title: How to convert urban energy balance into contributions to urban excess temperatures?
author: Hertel, Schlink

steps.title: Run ENVI‑met simulation
steps.instruction: Execute ENVI‑met (version 3.1) for the neighbourhood of interest, setting the initial wind speed to at least 3 m s⁻¹ (lower values cause numerical instability). Assign the specific humidity at 2500 m (top of model atmosphere) from radio‑soundings. Choose lateral boundary conditions based on the site: open for temperature and specific humidity, forced for turbulent kinetic energy. Test alternative boundary‑condition combinations to obtain the most accurate simulation. After the run, read the binary output files with the provided R code.

steps.title: Extract variables for Eq 9
steps.instruction: Using the R code supplied with the workflow, extract all model variables required by Equation 9 from the ENVI‑met binary files.

steps.title: Calculate ΔT contributions
steps.instruction: Apply Equation 9 to the extracted variables to compute the individual contributions to the Urban Heat Island intensity (ΔT).

steps.title: Visualise ΔT contributions
steps.instruction: With the same R environment, use the image.plot function to generate spatial contour plots of each ΔT contribution (e.g., radiative energy). Extend the visualisation to the remaining terms of the decomposition as needed.

description: Attribution techniques are defined as methods “…evaluating the relative contributions of multiple causal factors to a change or event…” [1]. Typically they are used for decomposing climate change into its causes and determining the magnitude of the anthropogenic contribution. Such techniques can be utilised for different changes or events whereby one of them is the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect that represents a temperature difference between urban and rural areas. The identification of dominant factors to UHI can improve the understanding of their dynamics and formation. Often, UHI attribution focuses on the city scale [2,3] or only on the respective contributions of the surface energy balance (SEB) terms. The specific underlying processes responsible for that and their caused temperature change are not considered (e.g. [4]). At smaller scales, like building levels, the urban geometry becomes very complex, which confines such investigations to single objects or street canyons with predefined orientations. The focus on the identification of dominant processes again lacks of a statement to the caused temperature change (e.g. [5]). In the present publication, we deduce a method for decomposing the Urban Heat Island intensity (ΔT) at the neighbourhood scale. The procedure is guided by a previously published approach [6]. In addition we share and describe an R [9] code especially developed for the decomposition scheme.
